cover.title: Neurodiversity and disability in figures
lede: There is no single official figure for ‘neurodivergent people worldwide’. Major international organisations do not use neurodivergence as a homogeneous statistical category: they measure specific conditions, disability, functioning, support needs, diagnosis, identification or social participation.

This section brings together figures that can be cited with precision. Each page states what was measured, in whom, where, when and using which source. When two figures seem contradictory, the first step is to check whether they are really measuring the same thing.

p: Autism · modelled global prevalence, differences in identification, diagnosis and comparison between countries. ADHD and learning · childhood and adult ADHD, dyslexia, coordination, Tourette syndrome, language, dyscalculia and dysgraphia. Mental health · anxiety, OCD and coexistence with autism. Disability and childhood · health, education, wellbeing, discrimination and access to support. Work and income · employment, labour-force participation and pay gap. European Union · employment, education, training, poverty and discrimination. Countries · United States, United Kingdom, Australia and Canada with national official sources. Methodological comparison · how to read international figures without creating false rankings.

A high or low figure does not, by itself, mean that a condition is more or less common in a country. It may change because the age studied, access to diagnosis, available records, the definition, the survey or the statistical method change. That is why each page keeps its context and explains what should not be concluded from it.

The main sources are WHO, UNICEF, ILO/ILOSTAT, Eurostat, CDC, GOV.UK, the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the Public Health Agency of Canada and selected international scientific reviews from the underlying research base.
Last editorial review of this document: 1 September 2026.

reglas: Each `PAGE` block can become an independent page within the Data tab.
Always keep territory + population + year of the data + method + source together.
Do not add together prevalences of neurodivergent conditions: there is overlap between them.
Do not use disability as a synonym for neurodivergence.
Do not turn figures about children into figures for the whole population.
Do not mix registered diagnosis, identification, survey data, meta-analysis and modelled prevalence.
Do not round or change denominators unless the entry itself says so.
Mental health figures appear because they are part of the knowledge base and may coexist with neurodivergent conditions; they are not presented as a synonym for neurodivergence.

paginas.title: Autism

lede.text: In 2021, an estimated 61.8 million people —approximately 1 in every 127— were autistic worldwide. This is a modelled estimate from Global Burden of Disease 2021, not a count of diagnoses. WHO currently uses this figure and notes that observed prevalence varies widely between studies and remains unknown in many low- and middle-income countries.

paginas.refTemporal: 2021 · 2025; WHO updates the fact sheet in 2025.
paginas.publicacion: 2025; WHO updates the fact sheet in 2025
paginas.poblacion: autistic people estimated in 2021

b.text: The Global Burden of Disease 2021 study estimated 61.8 million autistic people worldwide, with an uncertainty interval of 52.1 to 72.7 million.
That is approximately equivalent to:
Global age-standardised prevalence was estimated at 788.3 per 100,000 people.

mide.text: The figure attempts to estimate autism prevalence across all ages worldwide through epidemiological modelling. It can therefore approximate populations where no complete diagnostic register exists, but it should not be confused with the number of diagnoses issued by health or education services.

citar.text: Cite it as a modelled global estimate, not as a count of diagnoses. Keep together 61.8 million, 1 in 127, the year 2021 and the GBD/WHO reference.

evitar.text: The previous GBD 2019 estimate was much lower. The study itself explains that a significant part of the difference is due to methodological changes, including no longer relying on passive-identification studies that may have underestimated prevalence. The jump between GBD 2019 and GBD 2021 should therefore not be presented as a real increase in autism in just two years.

paginas.title: Autism: sex differences in the global estimate

lede.text: The GBD 2021 global model estimated 1,064.7 autistic people per 100,000 males and 508.1 per 100,000 females. These are modelled epidemiological estimates and are not equivalent to the proportion of diagnoses recorded by health or education services.

paginas.revision: Every 2 years or when GBD changes
paginas.poblacion: age-standardised prevalence in males

b.text: GBD 2021 estimated a modelled prevalence approximately twice as high in males as in females.

mide.text: The comparison uses age-standardised rates from the same global model. It is useful for observing an estimated difference between males and females and, when compared with higher diagnostic ratios, for showing that identification and prevalence are not exactly the same thing.

Diagnostic ratios are often higher than this modelled difference. A review of 54 studies and more than 13.7 million participants found that the male:female ratio was 4.20:1 when all studies were pooled, but fell to 3.25:1 in studies that screened the general population instead of starting only from already existing diagnoses.
This is compatible with identification bias: diagnostic figures do not measure prevalence alone.

citar.text: Always state that the sex-specific rates are age-standardised modelled estimates. Do not present them as a global diagnostic ratio or as a closed biological difference.

evitar.text: The figure must remain linked to its population, territory, year and method. Separating it from that context can change its meaning.

paginas.title: Autism: population health burden

lede.text: In 2021, the Global Burden of Disease model estimated 11.5 million DALYs associated with autism. This measure is used to study population-level health burden; it does not describe the experience, quality of life or individual needs of an autistic person.

paginas.revision: Every 2 years or when GBD changes
paginas.poblacion: GBD model population for 2021, not a count of people

b.text: GBD 2021 estimated that autism accounted for 11.5 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) in 2021.

mide.text: DALYs are a measure of population health burden. They are used to compare conditions within GBD models; they do not indicate how many years a specific person loses, nor do they summarise quality of life, autonomy, support needs or strengths.

A DALY is a measure of population health burden. It does not mean that an autistic person literally ‘loses’ a specific number of years of life. It combines years of life lost due to premature mortality and years lived with disability according to the GBD model.

For autism, this figure must be used very cautiously because it depends on the model’s disability weights and does not describe strengths, individual quality of life or the specific needs of a person.

citar.text: If the DALY figure is used, explain what a DALY is. Do not translate it into ‘years of life lost for each autistic person’ and do not use it as an individual measure of quality of life.

evitar.text: The figure must remain linked to its population, territory, year and method. Separating it from that context can change its meaning.

paginas.title: Developmental disability in children and young people

lede.text: In 2019, approximately 317 million children and young people worldwide were living with health conditions that contribute to developmental disability. The joint WHO and UNICEF report also points to barriers in healthcare, stigma, prejudice and social exclusion.

paginas.poblacion: children, adolescents and young people affected in 2019

cifras.pie: children, adolescents and young people living with those conditions in 2019

b.text: WHO and UNICEF estimated that in 2019 approximately 317 million children and young people were living with health conditions that contribute to developmental disability.

mide.text: The figure groups together children and young people with health conditions that contribute to developmental disability. The framework is broader than autism, ADHD or any other specific neurodivergent condition, so it cannot be turned into a global count of neurodivergence.

citar.text: Cite ‘health conditions that contribute to developmental disability’. Do not replace that wording with ‘317 million neurodivergent children’.

evitar.text: This figure does not mean 317 million neurodivergent children. The framework includes a broad set of congenital or acquired conditions that may lead to developmental disability.

paginas.title: Why comparable developmental data are missing

lede.text: Not all figures described as ‘global’ represent every region in the same way. A 2023 international review concluded that, for several developmental disabilities, geographical coverage was insufficient and methods were too heterogeneous for the estimates to be considered fully representative of the planet.

paginas.refTemporal: reviews included up to publication · umbrella review, 2023.
paginas.poblacion: Studies from high-income countries, using methods that differ from one another

cifrasIntro.text: A 2023 umbrella review examined global estimates for ADHD, autism, cerebral palsy, developmental intellectual disability, epilepsy, hearing loss, visual loss and dyslexia.
Its conclusion is important for the Data tab:
> Many estimates labelled as ‘global’ come from samples concentrated in high-income countries and show substantial methodological heterogeneity.

mide.text: This page does not count a population: it assesses how representative the available evidence is. The review shows that a figure called global may rely mainly on studies from high-income countries and on methods that differ widely from one another.

citar.text: This page does not provide a prevalence estimate: it documents a limitation in the global evidence. It should be cited as a methodological warning.

evitar.text: The figure must remain linked to its population, territory, year and method. Separating it from that context can change its meaning.

lede.text: An international umbrella review bringing together 588 studies and more than 3.27 million participants estimated a pooled ADHD prevalence of 8.0% in children and adolescents. The figure was 10% in boys and 5% in girls.

mide.text: The 8.0% figure summarises results from hundreds of studies included in previous reviews. It is a pooled prevalence, useful for understanding the order of magnitude of ADHD in children and adolescents, but it is not equivalent to a worldwide administrative diagnostic rate.

citar.text: Present 8.0% as the pooled prevalence from an umbrella review, with its 95% CI and the size of the evidence base. Do not present it as worldwide registered diagnosis.

evitar.text: It is not a worldwide census or a WHO statistic. It is a pooled estimate from studies using different methods. It should appear as a meta-analysis, not as ‘8% of all children in the world have an ADHD diagnosis’.

paginas.title: ADHD in adults

lede.text: An international meta-analysis estimated a 2020 prevalence of 2.58% for adult ADHD persisting from childhood, equivalent to about 139.84 million adults. When a definition of symptomatic adult ADHD was used without requiring proof of childhood onset, the estimate was 6.76%, about 366.33 million. These are different definitions and should not be presented as a single figure.

mide.text: The meta-analysis builds two estimates because it uses two definitions of adult ADHD. One requires persistence from childhood and the other is based on adult symptoms without requiring proof of that onset; this is why the percentages and resulting millions are different.

citar.text: Keep the two definitions separate: ADHD persisting from childhood (2.58%) and symptomatic adult ADHD (6.76%). Do not add or average the two figures.

evitar.text: The figure must remain linked to its population, territory, year and method. Separating it from that context can change its meaning.

mide.text: The indicator summarises studies of primary-school pupils and allows comparisons, within the meta-analysis, by sex and writing system. It does not automatically describe adult prevalence or guarantee the same rate in every language or country.

citar.text: Cite 7.10% as a pooled estimate in primary-school pupils. Do not automatically extrapolate it to all ages or to every country.

paginas.title: Developmental coordination disorder

lede.text: A systematic review and meta-analysis published in 2024 estimated a pooled prevalence of 5% for developmental coordination disorder in the general child population. Variation between studies was high, so the figure should be read as a scientific synthesis and not as an identical rate for all countries.

paginas.poblacion: pooled prevalence in children

b.text: A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis included 18 articles and 31,203 participants. For the general child population, pooled prevalence was 5%.
Meta-analysis subgroups:

mide.text: The 5% figure is a synthesis of studies of the general child population. The subgroups by sex and region help explore variation, but high heterogeneity means they should not be treated as definitive geographical differences.

citar.text: Cite 5% as pooled childhood prevalence from the meta-analysis. Regional figures are subgroups with high heterogeneity and should not be used to rank continents.

evitar.text: Heterogeneity between studies was very high. Regional differences come from few studies and should not be used as a geographical ranking.

paginas.title: Tourette syndrome: estimated prevalence and identification

lede.text: Tourette syndrome clearly shows the difference between estimated prevalence and recorded identification. CDC summarises studies placing childhood prevalence at around 0.6%, while parent-reported diagnosis in the United States was lower.

paginas.anioDatos: synthesis of studies; reported diagnosis in the U.S. 2016–2019
paginas.metodo: Official United States statistics or surveillance
paginas.poblacion: The two figures do not share a denominator: the parent-reported diagnosis figure is for ages 3 to 17; the studies figure does not restrict age

b.text: CDC summarises studies that include diagnosed and undiagnosed children and estimates that approximately 1 in 162 children (0.6%) have Tourette syndrome.
In the United States, parent-reported diagnosis data were lower:

cifras.den: Niños, sin tramo de edad especificado en la fuente; estimación de estudios que incluyen casos sin diagnosticar

mide.text: This page contrasts two ways of measuring: studies that try to capture diagnosed and undiagnosed cases, and a U.S. survey based on parent-reported diagnosis. The difference between 0.6% and 0.3% illustrates why prevalence and recorded identification are not synonyms.
Estimated prevalence from active studies may be higher than the number of recorded diagnoses. Identification and prevalence are not synonyms.

citar.text: Distinguish between the estimate from studies that include diagnosed and undiagnosed cases (0.6%) and parent-reported diagnosis in the U.S. (0.3%).

evitar.text: The figure must remain linked to its population, territory, year and method. Separating it from that context can change its meaning.

paginas.title: Developmental language disorder: a reference population study

lede.text: For developmental language disorder, no single global prevalence has been selected. This page uses a reference British population study to show a robust figure with defined population and method, without turning it into a global estimate.

paginas.refTemporal: sample of children entering school · British population study, 2016.
paginas.revision: Every 2 years; look for a new synthesis
paginas.poblacion: Children entering school, British population sample, 2016

b.text: A widely cited British population study estimated a prevalence of 7.58% for language disorder of then-unknown origin in children entering school.

mide.text: The 7.58% figure comes from a British population study of children entering school. It is useful because it clearly defines the population studied, but it was not designed as a representative estimate for every country in the world.

citar.text: Cite 7.58% as the result of a British population study of children entering school. Do not label it as global prevalence of DLD.

evitar.text: The figure must remain linked to its population, territory, year and method. Separating it from that context can change its meaning.

paginas.title: Dyscalculia and dysgraphia: why we do not give a single global figure

lede.text: The literature uses different definitions, tests, ages and thresholds. Widely repeated ranges exist, but the search carried out for this expansion did not find a recent international estimate with robustness comparable to the sources selected for ADHD, dyslexia or developmental coordination disorder.

paginas.refTemporal: no single year: no selected global figure exists · editorial review of sources, 2026.
paginas.anioDatos: no single year: no selected global figure exists
paginas.poblacion: No single figure

b.text: The evidence located uses different definitions, tests, ages and thresholds. The editorial decision is not to turn that variation into a single worldwide percentage until a recent international synthesis with comparable methodology is available.

mide.text: The important point on this page is methodological: no sufficiently comparable single global figure has been selected. Dyscalculia and dysgraphia are studied using different ages, tests, definitions and cut-off points; publishing a single percentage without explaining those differences would imply a precision that the selected evidence does not allow.

citar.text: The publishable conclusion is precisely that no single global figure is selected. Do not fill this block with ranges from general-information pages that lack comparable methodology.

evitar.text: The figure must remain linked to its population, territory, year and method. Separating it from that context can change its meaning.

notaFuentes: La investigación base no seleccionó una fuente única con solidez comparable a las utilizadas para TDAH, dislexia o trastorno del desarrollo de la coordinación. Antes de añadir una cifra, debe localizarse una revisión internacional reciente con definición, población, método y criterio de corte explícitos.

paginas.title: Anxiety disorders

lede.text: Anxiety disorders are the most common mental disorders worldwide. WHO estimates that in 2021 they affected 359 million people, including 72 million minors, and that around 27.6% of those who need treatment receive it.

paginas.poblacion: people with an anxiety disorder in 2021

Among the 359 million people in 2021 there were:

mide.text: WHO combines a global estimate of people with anxiety disorders in 2021 with an indicator of the treatment gap. The page distinguishes how many people are estimated to be affected from how many receive care among those who need it.

citar.text: Cite 359 million and 4.4% as WHO estimates for 2021. If the 27.6% figure is used, clarify that it refers to the proportion of people who need treatment who receive some form of treatment.

evitar.text: Anxiety is not a synonym for neurodivergence. It is included because it often appears as a coexisting condition and because it is part of the Iris Green knowledge base.

paginas.title: OCD

lede.text: There is no single global prevalence figure for OCD independent of diagnostic criteria. An international study published in 2026 estimated lifetime prevalence between 2.28% and 3.21%, depending on the diagnostic system used.

paginas.poblacion: Lifetime prevalence, by diagnostic system

cifrasIntro.text: A systematic review and modelling study published online on 8 July 2026 brought together 112 studies representative of national or subnational populations.
The estimated global lifetime prevalence depended on the diagnostic criteria:

mide.text: The review estimates lifetime prevalence and shows that the result depends on the diagnostic system applied. The four figures do not compete with one another: each one corresponds to different criteria.
It shows that even the same condition can produce different figures depending on the criterion used. The statistical definition matters.

citar.text: State that lifetime prevalence changes according to diagnostic criteria. The range 2.28–3.21% is not a confidence interval for a single figure.

evitar.text: The figure must remain linked to its population, territory, year and method. Separating it from that context can change its meaning.

mide.text: The percentages represent pooled prevalences of coexisting conditions within samples of autistic people. They are useful for showing that care cannot be reduced to a single label, but they do not predict what will happen for any one person.

citar.text: Present the percentages as pooled prevalences of coexisting conditions in a meta-analysis. They are not individual probabilities and heterogeneity was very high.

evitar.text: Unexplained heterogeneity was very high —I² above 95%— and figures changed according to age, sex, intellectual functioning, country and type of sample. Clinical studies produced higher prevalences than population-based or registry studies.

paginas.title: Significant disability

lede.text: More than 1.3 billion people —around 16% of the world population, 1 in 6— live with a significant disability.

paginas.refTemporal: current global estimate · WHO Europe, update 10-08-2026.
paginas.poblacion: people

b.text: WHO keeps this estimate in its European update of 10 August 2026.

mide.text: WHO uses a broad category of significant disability. It is contextual data for studying barriers in health, education, employment and participation; it is not an estimate of the neurodivergent population.

citar.text: Cite 1.3 billion, 16% and 1 in 6 as three ways of expressing the same estimate. Do not use ‘disability’ as a synonym for ‘neurodivergence’.

evitar.text: Disability is not a synonym for neurodivergence. This figure is used to describe barriers in health, education, employment, mobility and participation affecting the disabled population, within which part of the neurodivergent population is included.

paginas.title: Health inequality associated with disability

lede.text: Health differences associated with disability are not explained only by underlying conditions. WHO identifies health-service barriers, inaccessible transport, poverty, stigma and exclusion from education and employment as factors that produce avoidable inequality.

b.text: Some disabled people die up to 20 years earlier than non-disabled people as a result of inequalities and preventable conditions.

mide.text: The indicators summarise avoidable health and access inequalities associated with disability. They include mortality, noncommunicable diseases and physical or economic barriers; they do not describe inevitable consequences of a disability.

citar.text: These figures describe health inequalities and barriers associated with disability. They should not be interpreted as inevitable effects of an individual condition.

lede.text: Almost 240 million children —approximately 1 in 10— live with a disability worldwide. UNICEF’s analysis uses a broad functional approach and is not equivalent to counting medical diagnoses.

paginas.title: Employment and disability

lede.text: In an ILOSTAT comparison based on 61 countries, around one third of working-age persons with disabilities were employed, approximately half the proportion observed among persons without disabilities. The figure is an unweighted international average, not a single global rate.

paginas.poblacion: Persons with and without disabilities in 61 countries

b.text: working-age persons with disabilities were employed in the ILOSTAT comparative base.
This was approximately half the proportion observed among persons without disabilities.
persons with disabilities were outside the labour force, compared with 4 in 10 persons without disabilities.

mide.text: ILOSTAT compares the labour-market situation of persons with and without disabilities in 61 countries. The average is unweighted: each country contributes to the average without adjustment for population size.
The ILO specifies that these figures are based on the unweighted average of 61 countries. They are not a world rate weighted by population.

citar.text: The figure comes from the unweighted average of 61 countries. This must be stated explicitly: it is not a population-weighted world rate.

evitar.text: The figure must remain linked to its population, territory, year and method. Separating it from that context can change its meaning.

paginas.title: Pay gap and disability

lede.text: The pay gap associated with disability is not limited to access to employment. An international ILO study found an average difference in hourly pay even after taking variables such as age, education and occupation into account.

paginas.refTemporal: international subsample of 30 countries · ILO Working Paper 124, 27-08-2024.
paginas.poblacion: Hourly wages of workers with and without disabilities, international subsample

b.text: An ILO study published in 2024 found that, on average, employees with disabilities earned 12% less per hour than employees without disabilities in the international subsample analysed.
Approximately 9 percentage points could not be explained by the differences in age, education and occupation included in the model.
In that subgroup, the average pay gap reached 26%.

mide.text: The ILO compares hourly wages of workers with and without disabilities in an international subsample. The analysis also estimates how much of the difference remains after considering age, education and occupation.

citar.text: The 12% figure is the average for an international subsample of 30 countries. Do not attribute it to every country in the world or to all persons with disabilities.

evitar.text: The 12% result comes from a subsample of 30 countries, not from every country in the world.

mide.text: The employment gap subtracts the employment rate of persons with disabilities from the employment rate of those without disabilities. The correct unit is therefore percentage points, not a relative percentage.

citar.text: Use percentage points, not ‘24.2% less’. A gap of 24.2 points compares two employment rates.

evitar.text: A difference expressed in percentage points should not be turned into a relative percentage without recalculating it.

paginas.title: Labour-force participation and disability

lede.text: Participating in the labour market means either working or looking for work. In the European Union, 2024 data show a wide difference between persons with and without disabilities, and especially low participation among people with severe disabilities.

paginas.poblacion: Labour force: being outside the labour force is not the same as unemployment

of persons without disabilities.
Among people with severe disabilities, approximately one third participated; among those with a moderate limitation, approximately two thirds did.

mide.text: This indicator measures labour-market participation, that is, being employed or actively looking for employment. A person outside the labour force is not classified in the same way as an unemployed person who is looking for work.

citar.text: Distinguish labour-force participation from employment: participation means working or looking for work. They are not the same rate.

evitar.text: Labour-market participation and employment are different indicators.

paginas.title: Poverty and social exclusion

lede.text: In the EU, persons with disabilities are more exposed to poverty and social exclusion. In 2024, 28.8% were at risk of poverty or social exclusion, compared with 17.9% of persons without activity limitation.

mide.text: The European indicator of risk of poverty or social exclusion brings together different dimensions. Secondary data —risk of poverty, material deprivation and low work intensity— help explain the overall picture, but they overlap and should not be added together.

citar.text: Always cite the age —16 years or over— and distinguish risk of poverty/exclusion from its components. Do not add the secondary indicators together.

evitar.text: Poverty and exclusion indicators overlap; they should not be added together.

lede.text: In 2022, CDC’s ADDM Network identified autism in 32.2 per 1,000 8-year-old children —approximately 1 in 31— in 16 U.S. communities. It is one of the most cited autism data points and also one of the most often taken out of context.

mide.text: ADDM is a records-based surveillance network. It looks for evidence of autism in health and education records for children of a specific age and in specific communities; it is not a national survey of all ages.

citar.text: It must appear in full: 8-year-old children, 2022 surveillance, 16 ADDM communities and 32.2 per 1,000. Do not write ‘1 in 31 people in the U.S.’.

mide.text: The Buckland Review compares employment among autistic people of working age with employment among disabled people overall and non-disabled people. It is a snapshot of the UK labour market using the latest data available to the review.
